name: the buried branch
title: Fixing the garden irrigation timer
readme: Synthetic analogue of the kind of case Zach described: a conversation whose title and dominant topic are unrelated to a valuable conceptual branch. All text is invented for this repo.
Dominant topic: 40 turns on a drip line, a valve schedule and a leaking connector.
Buried branch: turns 17-23. The user defines an idea (U-19), the assistant extends it (A-20), the user accepts part and rejects the rest (U-21), and the user names it (U-23).
Second island: turns 34-35, where the user refers back to the named idea. It must come back as its own segment.
Distractors: 'routing' in the plumbing sense at U-5 and A-28. They should anchor on lexical search and be placed adjacency.
Alternate: A-20' is a regenerated-away sibling of A-20 proposing a different name. Its unique text must be findable as an alternate and never merged into the active-branch segment.
Design rules exercised: segment-retrieval note sections 3.2-3.5 (anchors, boundaries, distinctness) and the fixture plan's F-00 scores.
turns: My garden irrigation timer stopped running the morning cycle. Where should I start?
Start with power and the clock: check the battery, then confirm the timer's date and program are still set.
Battery is new and the clock is right. Program A says 6:00 for zones 1 to 3.
Then check whether the valves get the signal. Run zone 1 manually and listen for the solenoid click.
Zone 1 clicks. I think the problem is the routing of the drip line past the shed, it bends twice.
Two bends are fine for half-inch drip tubing. A sharp kink is not. Is the line flattened anywhere?
No kinks. Pressure at the far emitters is weak though.
Weak far-end pressure usually means a leak upstream or too many emitters on one zone.
There are about 40 emitters on zone 2. The connector at the tee drips constantly.
Forty two-litre emitters is within range for most zones. Fix the dripping tee first, it may be stealing the pressure.
The tee is a compression fitting. Do I cut the tube back?
Yes. Cut a clean square end about two centimetres back and push it fully into the fitting.
Done. The drip stopped. Far emitters are better but still uneven.
Uneven flow on a long run is normal on slopes. Pressure-compensating emitters even it out.
The bed slopes toward the fence. I'll swap the last ten emitters.
Good plan. Put the compensating ones at the high end.
Watching the water today I noticed it finds paths nobody planned. It pools where the soil is soft, not where I laid the line.
Water follows the least resistance, so the soil decides more than the layout does.
That's how work moves in a team's task queue too. I'd define emergent routing as tasks flowing to whoever has the least resistance right now, not to the person the plan assigned.
You could extend emergent routing in two ways: let the queue reassign tasks automatically by measured load, and publish a daily map of where tasks actually flowed.
Keep the daily flow map, that is useful. No automatic reassignment: people should still choose, the routing has to stay emergent.
So the map shows the paths and people keep the choice. The routing is observed, not imposed.
Yes. I'll call it seepage routing: the task queue as soil, the team as water.
Noted. Back to the bed: do you want a second zone for the slope?
Maybe. What would a second zone need?
A second valve on the manifold, a wire to a free station on the timer, and a new program line.
The timer has two free stations. How do I plan the tubing?
Plan the routing of the new line along the fence and keep the run under thirty metres, so the pressure holds at the far end.
Thirty metres is plenty. Which valve size?
Three-quarter-inch matches your manifold. Use the same brand so the solenoids interchange.
Bought it. The timer needs a program for zone 4 now.
Program B at 6:30 for zone 4, twenty minutes, so it does not overlap zones 1 to 3.
Set. It feels like the schedule should adapt to the weather on its own.
A rain sensor can skip cycles. Do you want the schedule to adjust itself beyond that?
No, same principle as seepage routing: show me where the water went and I decide the changes.
Then a soil-moisture readout per zone gives you the map without automatic changes.
Good. Anything else to check on the new valve?
Check the solenoid wire nuts are waterproof and the valve box drains.
Wire nuts are gel-filled. The box sits on gravel.
Then the system is in good shape. Run each zone once and watch the far emitters.
